FTSE-100 close CRUDE OIL
Nikkei-225 latest $22.70 per bbl
Blue-chip stocks edged higher and bonds jumped Friday as a strengthening dollar spurred foreign buying of U.S. assets.
After a volatile session, the Dow Jones industrial average ended up 1.16 points at 6,304.87, steadying after back-to-back losses totalling 170 points. For the week, the Dow lost 77.07 points.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,418 to 1,033 on active volume of 454 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Right from the opening bell, the Dow charted a frenzied course, sliding more than 50 points only to reverse course and later surge to a 40-point gain.
"The final analysis is -- it's been a rocky week," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities.
Analysts said computerized programme trading spurred the volatility as the market tried to find its footing after being rocked by a rapid rise in long-term bond interest rates.
The bond market also helped to shore up stocks.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond rose 20/32, or $6.25 per $1,000 face value. Its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, fell to 6.58 percent from 6.62 percent at Thursday's close.

"Bonds are back up which definitely helped the market," said Ricky Harrington, technical analyst at Interstate/Johnson Lane. "This morning we had extreme volatility and that's been the case for eight or nine sessions now. That's likely to continue to be the case going into early 1997."

The Dow index briefly dipped in the afternoon after President Clinton played down fears that a stock market correction would hurt the economy. Some analysts, however, downplayed the signficance of Clinton's comments on the stock market.

"I think Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan has decided jawboning is better than using monetary policy and it looks like Clinton has decided to pick up on that," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist of Legg Mason Wood Walker.
"I don't think Clinton has the same credibility," he said. "People will view it as a political statement."
Last week, Greenspan rattled global markets after he said the central bank needed to be wary when "irrational exuberance" infects markets because that could end up damaging the economy.
The dollar rose to 113.90 Japanese yen and 1.5545 German marks in late trading from 113.17 yen and 1.5410 marks late Thursday.
Oil prices rebounded as forecasts for colder weather across much of the country boosted demand for heating fuel.

On the New York Mercantile Exchange, January crude oil jumped 75 cents to $24.47 a barrel, though the contract still lost $1.18 on the week. January heating oil jumped 3.04 cents to 71.71 cents a gallon, and January gasoline rose 2.32 cents to 67.04 cents a gallon.
January natural gas rallied to a new contract high of $3.851 for 1,000 cubic feet, up 32.2 cents.
Fears that freezing weather would reach Florida's orange groves lifted March orange juice 1.50 cents to 96 cents a pound at the New York Cotton Exchange.

Overseas, London's FTSE, still under the spell of Wall Street after last Friday's sell-off, ended 18.3 points lower at 3,972.4, a gain of 9.4 from last Friday. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 finished down 159.81 points, or 0.78 percent, at 20,341.39, up 64.69 since last Friday.
